title: India's Deeptech Startups Draw Bigger Cheques as VC Funding Hits $1.1 Billion in Six Months
excerpt: Venture capital firms are writing larger cheques for Indian deeptech startups in 2026, with AI, defence, and space companies attracting institutional capital at a pace that could surpass last year's total.
body:
• Indian deeptech startups raised $1.1 billion in equity funding through the first half of 2026, already reaching nearly 80 per cent of the $1.4 billion raised in all of 2025, according to Tracxn data.
  • Neysa, an AI cloud acceleration startup, accounted for over half the capital with a $600 million Series B led by Blackstone, while Series A cheques in the sector have grown to $20-25 million.
  • A wave of dedicated deeptech funds has emerged, including Unicorn India Ventures' ₹1,200 crore Fund III, Speciale Invest's planned ₹1,400 crore growth fund, and government-backed initiatives like the ₹1 trillion Research, Development and Innovation Fund.
  • India now hosts over 4,200 deeptech startups, with more than 550 founded in 2025 alone, according to the Nasscom-Zinnov India Tech Startup Report.

The Numbers Tell the Story

India's venture capital ecosystem is placing its most aggressive bets yet on deeptech. According to data from startup intelligence platform Tracxn, Indian deeptech companies raised $1.1 billion in equity funding through the first half of 2026 — already approaching the $1.4 billion raised across all of 2025. What's changed isn't just the volume of capital but the size of individual cheques.

AI cloud acceleration platform Neysa drew the headline number, raising $600 million in its Series B round led by Blackstone in February. But the shift runs deeper. Series A cheques have expanded significantly, with multiple startups securing rounds north of $20 million: Deccan AI raised $25 million, AI cloud platform Nava pulled in $22 million, electric motorcycle manufacturer Zeno secured $20.5 million, and spacetech startup Bellatrix Aerospace closed at $20 million.

A New Class of Deeptech Funds

The capital is flowing from a growing roster of dedicated deeptech vehicles. Unicorn India Ventures closed its third fund at ₹1,200 crore, exceeding its ₹1,000 crore target, with backing from public sector institutions including SIDBI, SBI, and NABARD. The firm plans to back around 20 startups, with average ticket sizes of ₹10-15 crore.

Speciale Invest, which specialises in deeptech and AI/ML, is looking to raise a ₹1,400 crore growth fund to help early-stage companies access follow-on capital — historically a persistent struggle for deeptech startups with longer gestation periods. Yali Capital, advised by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, raised ₹893 crore in 2025.

"The key thing to remember is that it won't invest directly in startups. Instead, it stimulates the capital available to them by investing in fund managers, who in turn invest in startups."

— Ashwin Raghuraman, Co-founder, Bharat Innovation Fund

The government's ₹1 trillion Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund, announced in the 2025-26 budget with an initial allocation of ₹20,000 crore, is expected to further catalyse private investment. Spacetech firms have been among the first beneficiaries, receiving early disbursals through designated fund managers including the Technology Development Board and BIRAC.

Beyond Software: Where the Money Is Going

The composition of deeptech funding reveals a deliberate pivot away from software-only plays. Unicorn India Ventures said it is largely avoiding AI application-focused SaaS companies and instead concentrating on AI infrastructure — semiconductors, data centres, power systems, and enabling technologies. The fund is also exploring nuclear micro power generation as a potential enabler for AI-led growth.

India now hosts more than 4,200 deeptech startups, with over 550 founded in 2025 alone, according to the Nasscom-Zinnov India Tech Startup Report. Deeptech funding rose 37 per cent to $2.3 billion in 2025, with artificial intelligence accounting for roughly 91 per cent of capital deployed.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora in the U.S. and globally, the deeptech boom represents both an investment opportunity and a professional one. A notable trend is the rising number of academicians as startup founders — four to five companies backed by Unicorn India's Fund III are led by academics, reflecting a closer integration of university research and commercial enterprise. The Bharat Innovates 2026 programme recently showcased 120 Indian deep-tech startups at an international expo in Nice, France, signalling the sector's global ambitions.
nri_angle: Deeptech boom creates investment and professional opportunities for NRIs; rising academic-founder trend reflects closer university-industry integration.
